## Why This Is Asked

Tests understanding of how CPU frequency scaling and idle states interact with latency, and whether a candidate can propose actionable, observable mitigations that are safe in production.

## Key Concepts

- CPU frequency scaling and governors
- Deep C-states and idle control
- Per-CPU observability and thread pinning
- Observability-preserving mitigations

## Code Example

```bash
#!/bin/bash
while true; do
  date
  for c in /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_cur_freq; do
    printf "%s: %s\n" "$c" "$(cat "$c")";
  done
  sleep 1
done
```

## Follow-up Questions

- If spikes correlate with freq/idle but persist, what other subsystems to inspect? (scheduler pressure, I/O wait)
- How would you validate the mitigations without destabilizing services across NUMA nodes?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to diagnose production-like latency issues driven by memory behavior in a containerized Linux environment using only built-in tools. It emphasizes observable metrics, reproducible steps, and safe mitigations that don’t destabilize services.

## Key Concepts

- Memory pressure and swap thrash
- cgroups memory controllers and per-container limits
- RSS, resident memory, and meminfo interpretation
- Safe, observable mitigations (swappiness, container memory caps)

## Code Example

```bash
# Memory pressure indicators
free -m
vmstat 1 60
grep -i 'MemAvailable\|SwapTotal\|SwapFree' /proc/meminfo

# Top memory consumers
ps -eo pid,comm,rss --sort=-rss | head -n 10

# Map to memory cgroups
for pid in $(ps -eo pid --no-headers); do
  if [ -d "/proc/$pid" ]; then
    if awk -F: '/memory/ {print $3}' /proc/$pid/cgroup 2>/dev/null | grep -q memory; then
      echo "PID $pid belongs to memory cgroup"

  fi
done
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical, end-to-end diagnostic skills for real-world Linux infra issues: distinguishing IO-bound from CPU-bound latency, identifying bottlenecks across storage and network layers, and applying safe mitigations without breaking observability.

## Key Concepts
- IO scheduling and per-device queues
- Distinguishing storage vs network bottlenecks
- Safe, observable mitigations (scheduler changes, queue depths, CPU affinity)
- Network path diagnostics and NIC interrupt handling
- irqbalance conflicts with manual affinity tuning

## Code Example
```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Diagnostic workflow for IO latency spikes
# 1) Baseline metrics
iostat -dx 1 5 > baseline_iostat.log
pidstat -u 1 5 > baseline_cpu.log
ethtool -S eth0 | grep -E 'rx_bytes|tx_bytes|drop' > baseline_network.log

# 2) Identify bottleneck
if [[ $(iostat -dx 1 1 | awk '$NF > 80 {print $NF}') ]]; then
    echo "Storage bottleneck detected"
    echo deadline > /sys/block/sdX/queue/scheduler
    echo 128 > /sys/block/sdX/queue/nr_requests
fi

# 3) Verify fix
iostat -dx 1 10 > post_fix_iostat.log
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you automate this workflow for a fleet of nodes?
- What metrics would you export to central dashboard?
- When would you consider switching from iSCSI to NVMe-oF?
